title: D.C. Circuits
seo_title: Secondary 4 Physics: D.C. Circuits Worksheets (O-Level 6091 with Answers)
standard_text: Draw and interpret circuit diagrams with standard symbols; state that the current at every point in a series circuit is the same and that the sum of the p.d.s across the components equals the supply p.d.; state that in parallel circuits the current from the source is the sum of the branch currents and the p.d. across each branch is the same; recall and calculate effective resistance in series and in parallel; solve circuit problems using V = IR; describe the action of a potential divider and of thermistors and light-dependent resistors as input transducers (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Physics 6091 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 4 O-Level Physics worksheets on D.C. circuits: series and parallel circuits, effective resistance, solving circuits with V = IR, potential dividers, thermistors and LDRs. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Series: same current. Parallel: same p.d.
body_html:
How to think about it

Series and parallel circuits follow different rules.

  • Series: the same current everywhere; p.d.s add up to the supply p.d.; R = R₁ + R₂.
  • Parallel: the same p.d. across each branch; branch currents add up; 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂, so R is less than the smallest resistor.
  • Potential divider: Vout = Vin × R₂ ÷ (R₁ + R₂). A thermistor's resistance falls when hot; an LDR's falls in bright light.
Example

4 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel?

1/R = 1/4 + 1/12 = 4/12

Answer: 3 Ω

Example

2 Ω in series with (6 Ω ∥ 3 Ω), 12 V supply. Current?

pair = 2 Ω

total = 4 Ω

I = 12 ÷ 4

Answer: 3 A

Common mistakes

  • Adding parallel resistances like series ones.
  • Thinking the current is shared out along a series circuit.
  • Forgetting to take the reciprocal at the end of 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.
  • Saying an LDR's resistance rises in bright light.

faq.q: How do you find the effective resistance of resistors in parallel?
faq.a: Add the reciprocals: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂, then take the reciprocal of the answer. For two resistors, R = R₁R₂ ÷ (R₁ + R₂).

faq.q: How does a potential divider work?
faq.a: Two resistors in series share the supply p.d. in the ratio of their resistances, so the output across one of them is a fraction of the supply.

faq.q: How are thermistors and LDRs used in circuits?
faq.a: As one resistor in a potential divider: when temperature or light changes, their resistance changes, so the output p.d. changes and can switch on a device.

items.q: Three lamps are in series. The current through the first lamp is 0.5 A. What is the current through the third lamp?
items.e: In series the current is the same everywhere.

items.q: A parallel circuit has two branches. The currents in the branches are 0.2 A and 0.2 A. What is the current from the cell?
items.e: In parallel the branch currents add up: 0.2 + 0.2.

items.q: What is a potential divider used for?
c: to provide a fraction of the supply p.d. as an output
items.e: Two resistors in series share the p.d. in the ratio of their resistances.

items.q: An ammeter before the first of 3 lamps in a series circuit reads 1.2 A. What does an ammeter between the lamps read?
items.e: In series the current is the same everywhere. It is not used up.

items.q: Three lamps are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. What is the p.d. across each lamp?
items.e: In parallel each branch has the full supply p.d.

items.q: In a parallel circuit, how does the p.d. across each branch compare with the supply p.d.?
c: It is double the supply p.d.
It is equal to the supply p.d.
items.e: Each branch is connected directly across the supply.

items.q: Two lamps are in series with a 12 V battery. The voltmeter across one lamp reads 5 V. What does it read across the other lamp?
items.e: In series the potential difference is shared: 12 − 5.

items.q: Two resistors are in series with a 12 V supply. The p.d. across one is 8 V. What is the p.d. across the other?
items.e: In series the p.d.s add up to the supply p.d.: 12 − 8 = 4 V.

items.q: Two lamps are in series with a 9 V battery. The voltmeter across one lamp reads 4 V. What does it read across the other lamp?
items.e: In series the potential difference is shared: 9 − 4.

items.q: Three lamps are connected in parallel across a 9 V battery. What is the p.d. across each lamp?
items.e: In parallel each branch has the full supply p.d.

items.q: An ammeter before the first of 2 lamps in a series circuit reads 0.8 A. What does an ammeter between the lamps read?
items.e: In series the current is the same everywhere. It is not used up.

items.q: The current from the cell is 0.7 A. One of two parallel branches carries 0.3 A. What does the other branch carry?
Two lamps are in series with a 4.5 V battery. The voltmeter across one lamp reads 2 V. What does it read across the other lamp?
items.e: In series the potential difference is shared: 4.5 − 2.

items.q: What is the effective resistance of resistors in series?
items.e: R = R₁ + R₂ + …

items.q: Why are the lamps in a home connected in parallel?
c: So that if one fails, all go off.
So one switch controls them all.
Each gets the full mains p.d. and can be switched on or off on its own.
items.e: Parallel branches are independent.

items.q: A parallel circuit has two branches. The currents in the branches are 0.5 A and 0.7 A. What is the current from the cell?
items.e: In parallel the branch currents add up: 0.5 + 0.7.

items.q: Another resistor is added in parallel to a circuit. What happens to the total current from the supply?
items.e: The total resistance falls.

items.q: Two branches are in parallel. They carry 0.5 A and 0.8 A. What current flows from the supply?
items.e: Currents in parallel branches add up: 0.5 + 0.8 = 1.3 A.

items.q: In a series circuit with 2 lamps, the current leaving the cell is 0.6 A. What is the current returning to the cell?
items.e: In series the current is the same everywhere. It is not used up.

items.q: Two resistors are in series with a 6 V supply. The p.d. across one is 4 V. What is the p.d. across the other?
items.e: In series the p.d.s add up to the supply p.d.: 6 − 4 = 2 V.

items.q: Resistors of 3 Ω, 8 Ω and 20 Ω are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
items.e: In series, R total = R₁ + R₂ + …

items.q: Resistors of 4 Ω and 4 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the effective resistance?
items.e: 1/R = 1/4 + 1/4, so R = 2 Ω (less than the smallest resistor).

items.q: 4 identical 20 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the effective resistance?
items.e: n equal resistors in parallel: R = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 Ω.

c: It is largest after the last lamp.
It is the same at every point.
items.e: There is only one path.

items.e: 1/R = 1/3 + 1/6, so R = 2 Ω (less than the smallest resistor).

items.q: 5 identical 60 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the effective resistance?
items.e: n equal resistors in parallel: R = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 Ω.

items.q: How does the effective resistance of two resistors in parallel compare with each one?
c: It is less than the smaller of the two.
It is the sum of the two.
It is more than the larger one.
It is the same as the larger one.
items.e: Adding a parallel path lets more current flow.

items.q: Why does a voltmeter need a very high resistance?
c: So it can be connected in series.
So it takes almost no current and does not change the circuit it measures.
items.e: It is connected in parallel.

items.q: Two identical lamps are connected in series to a cell. A third identical lamp is added in series. How does the brightness of each lamp change?
items.e: The total resistance rises, so the current falls.

items.q: Resistors of 20 Ω and 30 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the effective resistance?
items.e: 1/R = 1/20 + 1/30, so R = 12 Ω (less than the smallest resistor).

items.q: Two 6 Ω resistors are in parallel, and this pair is in series with a 3 Ω resistor. What is the total resistance?
items.e: Pair = 3 Ω; 3 + 3 = 6 Ω.

items.e: 1/R = 1/5 + 1/20, so R = 4 Ω (less than the smallest resistor).

items.q: 2 identical 100 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the effective resistance?
items.e: n equal resistors in parallel: R = 100 ÷ 2 = 50 Ω.

items.q: A light sensor switches on street lights when it gets dark. Which input transducer is used?
items.e: The LDR's resistance rises in the dark.

items.e: Total R = 6 Ω; I = 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5 A.

items.e: Equal resistors share the p.d. equally.

Which arrangement of two 10 Ω resistors gives the smallest effective resistance?
items.e: Parallel gives less than either resistor.

items.q: Resistors of 12 Ω, 12 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the effective resistance?
A 6 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 12 Ω and 4 Ω resistors, connected to a 9 V supply. What is the potential difference across the 6 Ω resistor?
A potential divider is made of R₁ = 3 Ω (top) and R₂ = 1 Ω (bottom) across a 12 V supply. What is the output p.d. across R₂?
items.e: V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> × R₂ ÷ (R₁ + R₂) = 12 × 1 ÷ 4 = 3 V.

items.q: What happens to the resistance of a light-dependent resistor (LDR) when the light intensity increases?
items.e: Thermistors (NTC) and LDRs have resistances that fall as temperature or light intensity rises.

items.q: A potential divider has a fixed resistor and a sensor. The LDR is R₂ (bottom) and the light gets brighter. What happens to the output p.d. across R₂?
items.e: In bright light the LDR's resistance falls, so its share of the p.d. falls.

items.q: In a series circuit of two lamps, one lamp breaks. What happens?
c: The other lamp gets dimmer only.
The other lamp goes out because the circuit is broken.
items.e: One path only.

items.q: A potential divider has a fixed resistor and a sensor. The LDR is R₂ (bottom) and it gets darker. What happens to the output p.d. across R₂?
items.e: In the dark the LDR's resistance rises, so it takes a larger share of the p.d.

items.e: V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> × R₂ ÷ (R₁ + R₂) = 15 × 5 ÷ 6 = 12.5 V.

items.q: A potential divider has a fixed resistor and a sensor. The LDR is R₁ (top) and it gets darker; the output is across the fixed resistor R₂. What happens to the output p.d. across R₂?
items.e: The LDR's resistance rises, so the fixed resistor's share falls.
